whatItFakes: The Nation heading on News tells every law another state passed in the last nationNewsDays, not the ones a reader would care about.
why: Which other-state laws reach a player's attention needs an interest rule from the owner (the places the player has lived, the topics in their drives); until then a plain window over the records shows the country moving without a cap or a chance.
replacement: Resolved Nov 8 (State Sessions, the CTO's Nov 6 ruling): src/bench/nation-news.ts tells a law when its state's share of the nation times one plus the reader's family, work and neighbor ties clears nationNewsReachBar; the data is src/core2/data/places/state-reach.json (Census population and county adjacency).

whatItFakes: The Nation heading's reader ties are family, work and a neighboring state; a state the reader moved from is not a tie.
why: A person keeps no record of the places they have lived (no moved-from field in people or the life engine), so the tie cannot be read.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Read the reader's past homes once the people engine records them, and add it as a fourth term beside family, work and neighbor (nationNewsMovedTie).
resolvedBy: stand-in triage T9 (owner, Nov 10: too in depth)

whatItFakes: The paper's round-birthday and retirement briefs read only the town's full residents; a counted resident who turns 80, 90 or 100, or who retires, gets no notice.

replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A person a brief names is a named person, so the counted resident whose round birthday falls in the week is filled in, seeded from the world, when the notice prints (two-level population; the CTO, Nov 1, the same rule the lives lead uses), and the week's round birthdays are read from the counted population's ages by place by the same rule as a full resident.
resolvedBy: stand-in triage T9 (owner, Nov 10: too in depth)

whatItFakes: Only full readers write letters to the editor: a counted reader of the outlet never does.

resolvedBy: stand-in triage T9 (owner, Nov 10: too in depth)

replacement: The owner's ruling: either fewer choices are right, or OPUS-WORDS mines more answer moves per subject until three to five follow naturally.

The reply's other effects are real: the relative's yes to helping is counted among the campaign's volunteers, and a put-off lowers the tie.
replacement: A household limit the campaigns engine reads when the candidate gives their own money, with the reply naming it (pool item campaigns-household-limit-read).

whatItFakes: The clerk tells a candidate the office, the primary and general dates, the term and what the office does, but not how many petition signatures the filing needs: the clerk says nothing about signatures.
why: Owner, Oct 28 (sitting, 32, and the 2:10 PM ruling): filing is petition, signatures, the clerk's check, then the ballot. The petition record (signatures required and held, the deadline check, read from each place's rules) is the elections session's to build on its item; the words read that record once it exists. Resolved (Oct 29, 2026): once a filing is taken, the clerk says the signatures the petition record needs and the day they are due, or that the office takes no petition (filedAtCounter in src/director/filing-visit.ts, read from the elections engine's petitionOf). The signature scenes as the candidate campaigns are the next part of the plan's step 3, not a fact the clerk fakes.
replacement: The clerk's tell-signatures line reads the elections engine's petition record (signatures required, by place) and the signature scenes read its count as the candidate campaigns.

whatItFakes: A scene ending that keeps a promise or a favor is kept and settled only where data/promise-endings.json names its kind (src/core2/data/promises/promise-kinds.json names the record that settles it): a member's vote (the roll), paying on time after a money quarrel (the payments), showing a new coworker around (a talk). Every other ending that keeps a promise (a campaign pledge said at a scene, a constituent's call, a fix promised at the desk, a visit promised at a goodbye, and the rest) or a favor is kept as a fact and moves the tie by the talk's time only; nothing settles it.
why: Each kind needs the record that settles it named; some have one in another engine (a filing, a hire, a vote by question in record.ts) and some have no player act yet (reaching a relative or friend, going to a doctor: design-player-reaches-a-relative-or-friend, design-player-goes-to-a-doctor).
replacement: One row per ending in data/promise-endings.json, its kind naming the record that settles it, kept by the promises engine (src/core2/modules/promises.ts); a favor-owed ending is a view of the legislature's obligations row.

whatItFakes: At the recall table, the organizer's line that the member voted for the bill 'after telling us you wouldn't', and the member's two answers to it, need a promised-against fact; no engine records a promise to vote against a bill, so they never play and the organizer names only the vote.
why: Ask why: a broken promise is said only where a record holds the promise (a pledge, a platform stance against the bill's question, a reply in an earlier scene). The legislature records only a promise to vote for a bill (vote-promise, a committee trade).
replacement: purpose-scene sets promised-against for a recall petition when the member's filed platform takes the stand against the bill's question, or a scene reply recorded a promise against it, citing that record.

whatItFakes: Who gives the oath at a swearing-in. Real oaths are given by a judge, a justice or a notary (a state's chief justice swears in a governor); the world keeps no courts or notaries, so the oath is given by the clerk who took the winner's filing or keeps the government's papers, else the holder who left the seat that day, else the body's presiding officer. A clerk at the state level, and every fallback, marks this stopgap.
why: Courts come after early access (AGENTS.md). Ask why: the officiant is always a person a record names (the filing clerk, the town's or county's clerk, the seat's ended term, the leadership engine's presiding officer); with none on record the scene is not staged, and no one is invented.
replacement: The justice engine's judges and justices, cast by the court that swears in each office (a chief justice for a governor, a local judge for a council), read in oathGiver ahead of the clerk.

whatItFakes: The inaugural address of a mayor, county executive or governor is recorded as heard (speech.heard) only when the player plays their own swearing-in and chooses to speak; the world's other executives give no inaugural, because the office-day engine has only the annual address. The speech's occasion is read from its record id (speech:inaugural:...), as SG-DIRECTOR-speech-occasion reads every speech's.
why: The simulation should give the address for any sworn-in executive and the scene should read it (owner, Oct 29: the player's slice of a world event). The office-day engine's acts belong to the governing lead; the scene was built against the smallest stand-in. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: An inaugural act in the office-day engine, run for any sworn-in executive, that calls deliverSpeech with an occasion fact; the swearing-in scene then reads that record, and the existing address type stages it for the people who hear it.

whatItFakes: The counter's talk before filing (which office, the rules that stop a filing, the dates, the term and the duty) is still the filing visit's own sequence of moves, worded from the filing-clerk lines, rather than one scene of the scene engine. The clerk's talk after filing (the petition) is already the scheduled filing scene (purpose filing-petition). The filing-clerk tree lines (key routine: replies, follows and closes about a rival who filed) wait for that scene and play nowhere until then.
why: The plan approved Oct 28 (section 1) has the filing conversation fire through the one scheduler; the CTO (Nov 1, 16:05) kept the counter as the player's action screen for now and moved only the after-filing talk, so the golden path's filing step keeps working while the whole talk is built. Resolved Nov 13 (Words builder W3, Fable A's rulings of 04:19Z and 05:03Z on #8928): after the race is named, the counter's talk is one scene of the scene engine (composeSceneTalk, the filing-clerk arc: the race told, then file, ask, a rival or leave), each reply is a scene.reply record, and the next day's filing scene reads the reply that filed; the race pick and a rule refusal stay the counter screen's own steps.
replacement: A filing-clerk scene, caused by the player arriving at the office that takes filings, that plays the whole counter talk through the scene engine and ends by opening the counter screen (the filing-clerk arc's endings already open it); filing-visit.ts's own sequence is then deleted.

whatItFakes: A term is read from the web's rows twelve months after the world opened, because the town's records are still settling in before that (unemployment ran 0.3 percent to 5.7 percent and poverty 9.6 percent to 18.6 percent across the first twelve months of a played year in Algiers, Vermont, seed r7). The address and the groups' reactions therefore read no area of the term in a world's first fifteen months.
why: The economy's opening state is not a settled year, so a change from it reads as the official's doing. The fix is the economy's (the start of the town's jobs and incomes), not the term read's. The school measures are fixed (a cohort too small to measure reads the place's rate, #7391).
replacement: Laws and effects (or the economy lead) start the town's jobs and poverty measures from a settled year, after which the warm-up in src/core2/data/term-read/areas.json is zero and this stopgap is removed.

whatItFakes: A protest or strike that stands before a town official (type action-confront) is worded with the town hall's purpose (town-hall-question, reading host-declined). The narration, the protester's question, one follow and one close are the protest's own (they require the protest or strike fact); the official's replies and the endings are the town hall's, which say nothing of a crowd or a picket line.
why: The exchange is the same (a person with a demand, an official who answers) and the town hall's lines exist; the protest's own register (owner, Nov 8: the English works differently for different kinds of scenes) is the next piece of the Story lane.
replacement: A purpose of its own for action-confront in purpose-arcs.json whose replies and endings are stances toward the crowd (hear the line, send a representative, call the police, join them).

whatItFakes: A group's lobbyist who remembers how the player voted (circumstance lobby-remembers) says so, subtle or open by their own temper, and what the player answers is kept as a promise or a strained tie. The group's endorsement, gifts or a primary challenge do not move from it: the interest-group engine does not read the tie or the kept answer when it decides whom to back.
why: The threat is told and kept in the records the director already writes; making the group's backing follow the member's votes is the interest-group engine's decision, which no engine yet reads from a vote against the group (Laws and effects' area).
replacement: The interest-group engine reads the member's vote against its meeting and the kept tie when it decides endorsements and gifts; the scene then cites that decision.

The owner graded these lines good (owner, via the CTO, Nov 8: a rewrite never deletes a line he graded good); the engine that read their old bank was deleted, and the line is kept in a bank of its own kind until a scene reads it.

whatItFakes: The story-read scene's replies (agree, disagree, ask, put off) write the reply record, time together, a strain on the tie when the talk is put off or argued, the owed talk and the journal line; no engine moves the player's or the reader's view of the story's question from the talk.

whatItFakes: Which reason a farewell says when the departure record names several: the rows of departureWhy are tried in a hand-set order (an eviction, a job lost, a job elsewhere, family, kin who left first, a death), and a reason is said only when its row is present in the record.
why: The moves engine records every cause and push that built the pull, on scales that do not compare (events against pushes read on the holds' scale), so no one reason is 'the biggest'. Naming none when no row is present keeps the goodbye honest; the order is a hand-set stopgap. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: The moves engine records the one cause that tipped the pull over the holds (the largest term on a common scale) on the departure; the farewell reads that.

whatItFakes: Where a notice's lines call the shortfall small or deep: under half a month's rent is 'small', two months' rent or more is 'deep', and the lines for each differ.
why: Wording bands set by hand (TUNABLE, with a spread) from ordinary usage; no survey sizes at what share of a month's rent people say 'a little short' or 'months behind'. No outcome depends on them: the landlord's own weighing of amount and months is the housing engine's. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Bands read from how renters in the Household Pulse and the Eviction Lab describe arrears, or from the housing engine's own notice score so the lines follow the same weighing the landlord used.

whatItFakes: A scene whose moment never stopped the player's clock, and any scene for someone the player does not control, opens at the day's start minute instead of the minute its setting held it.
why: The director's scene carries no minute of its own; the moment records a date, not the hour the setting held it. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: The moment records the minute its setting opened it (ledger openedAt) and composeScene reads that.

whatItFakes: How strongly a speaker's traits tilt a governor's or mayor's address toward a kind. The mean of the kind's facet values is clamped to -1..1 though the facets run past it (a work-centered, meticulous governor's mean is 1.2), and the policy kind's base (policyBase 0.5, times the full agenda) doubles at the cap, so a speaker with a full list of asks and a work-centered turn scores policy 1.0 against a collapsing term's crisis 0.656 and gives the same address in a good term and a bad one (Greensboro, Maryland, seed f8fc37cc25201edc, official:term:seat:US-MD:governor:2025-01-20).
why: Calibration, not a clamp on the score: the policy score is raw (0.5 x work share x (1 + pull)) and, even unclamped (pull 1.2, score 1.1), is above crisis. Whether a full-agenda governor should still name a collapsing term is a Words call on policyBase, the pull scale and the crisis weight, which the owner has not ruled. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Words checks the address kinds against real State of the State addresses (a crisis term outweighs a long agenda), then sets policyBase and the pull's scale so a bad term can outscore policy for any speaker.

whatItFakes: The visit's limits as the narration says them: a guard stands by, the talk is through glass, the visit ends when the guard says. No facility, visiting rule or time limit is on a named prisoner's record, so the lines say these things for every visit, and none of them names a number of minutes.
why: The justice engine keeps custody (from, until, sentence) for a named person but not the facility, its kind or its visiting rules; only counted custody names a facility (jail, prison, juvenile). No pet is kept on any household record, so no visit asks after one. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: The justice engine records the facility and kind on a named prisoner's custody row (as it does for counted custody); the narration reads the kind and says the glass and the time only where that kind has them.

whatItFakes: What the visitor agrees to or promises in the prison visit (money on the prisoner's account, a child looked after, a lawyer called, a word taken to the family) is written on the reply record as a promise; no engine moves the money, makes the call or tells the family.
why: The justice engine has no commissary account or contact record for a named prisoner, and no hook reads a scene.reply of typeKey prison-visit. The visit still names the sentence or the bail from the record and a refusal pressed strains the tie. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A justice-engine account for a named prisoner that a promise of money pays into on the next day, and a people-engine owed-talk record for the word taken to the family.

whatItFakes: The visit scene's illness causes and a relative's visit to the player while the player is held have no scene of their own; a sick relative is covered by the care scene.
why: A visit to the ill needs the health engine's diagnosis and care records worded as the ask, and a visit to the player inside leaves the player no choices to reply with while they serve a term. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer. The visit type was then deleted with the scene inventory (Nov 12, 2026); prison-visit and care carry the visits that have purposes.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A hospital-visit purpose that reads the health engine's care need, and, for the player held, a letter or a call scene the player answers after release.

whatItFakes: A first meeting or a new friend's ask names the employer, the job, the school, the party and the town the two share. It never names a church, a club or a street, though people meet there.
why: No record in the world keeps a church, a club or a block for a person: memberships hold only parties (and groups the player joins), and a person's place is a town, not a street. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Memberships for congregations and clubs, and an address on the household record; meeting-facts.ts then reads them as it reads the party.

whatItFakes: The friend's invitation (dinner, a game, lunch, a drink after work) and favor (a couch, the mail, covering an afternoon, a pickup) are worded for every friend; nothing on a record says this friend plans a dinner or needs a hand. The facts around them (the shared employer, school, party, town) are from records.
why: No engine keeps what a person plans or needs from a friend; the plan is the ask itself, so the lines name only days and things any friend might ask. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A plans or needs record per person (a move coming, a child to pick up) that the ask reads, so the favor named is the one the records give.

whatItFakes: What the one who comes back wants from the player (to make up after a falling-out, to ask for a work lead, to tell news, to ask for a visit) is worded for every reunion; nothing on a record says this person wants a lead or a visit. How long they were away, where they live and what changed in their life are from records.
why: No engine keeps what a person wants from someone they have not seen in years; the ask is the purpose itself, so its lines name only things any returning friend or relative might ask, and lines about a falling-out play only when the pair's thread kept a soured turn. Resolved by deletion (Nov 12, 2026): the reunion scene was deleted with the scene inventory (docs/design/scene-inventory.md); no engine records a return.
replacement: A wants record per person (work sought, a quarrel to mend, news to tell) that the reunion reads, so the ask is the one the records give.

whatItFakes: The ask in a relative's letter (to come visit, to write or call, to hear their news) is worded for every letter; the `family.contact` record holds only who wrote and how close the two are. Where they live, what changed in their life since their last letter, a birthday they missed at the reader's table and their own birthday coming are from records.
why: The kin-contact engine writes a contact with no topic; nothing keeps what a relative wants to say, so the ask is the purpose and its lines name only things any relative might ask.
replacement: A topic on the contact record (a visit planned, news to share, a favor) drawn from the writer's own life records, so the letter asks what the records give.

whatItFakes: What a relative at a wedding or a new-job celebration asks of the player (a few words for everyone, a picture, a dance, a talk about an old quarrel, help finding work) is worded for every celebration; nothing on a record says this guest wants a toast or a picture. What is celebrated, whose it is, the guest's town, a new child, the guest being out of work and a quarrel on the tie are from records.
why: No engine keeps what a guest wants from a host at a family occasion; the ask is the purpose itself, so its lines name only things any relative at a celebration might ask, and lines about a quarrel, a new child or looking for work play only when a record says so.
replacement: A wants record per person (a favor to ask, a quarrel to mend, work sought) that the celebration reads, so the ask is the one the records give; birthdays and births as celebration causes once the director has a moment for them.

whatItFakes: What the household asks of the player after a birthday with a relative missing (to call, write, visit, make the first move, send word) is worded for every missed gathering; the `family.gathering-missed` record holds only who was missing, whose birthday it was and how close the two are. Whose birthday, the age, where the missing relative lives, their lately changed life and a quarrel on the tie are from records; why they did not come is never claimed.
why: The kin-contact engine writes the missed gathering with no reason; nothing keeps why a relative stayed away, so the lines say what the records show and ask the player to reach out, and never explain the absence.
replacement: A reason on the missed-gathering record (work, illness, distance, a falling-out) drawn from the absent relative's own life records, so the ask can name why.

whatItFakes: What the housemate who got the player help asks afterward (a ride to the doctor, a visit to one, to stay close, a promise to say when the player feels sick again, leave to tell the family, a word with a child who was in the room) is worded for every rescue; nothing on a record says this rescuer wants a visit to the doctor. That the rescuer got help, whether they are the player's partner, whether a child was in the room and whether other grown people saw it are from the rescue record, the family records and the witnesses; the illness itself is never named, because the rescue record does not say its kind.
why: No engine keeps what a person who helped in an emergency wants from the one they helped; the ask is the purpose itself, so its lines name only things anyone who called for help might ask, and lines about a partner, a child or the others at home play only when a record says so.
replacement: A wants record per person, and the health engine's case row (condition, how serious, the care it calls for) that the rescue reads, so the ask is the one the care needs.

whatItFakes: What the accused says to the person who reported them (that they will tell the whole of it, own up, or answer) is written on the reply record; no engine reads it, so an accused who owns up to the accuser is not treated any differently by the prosecutor's investigation. The accuser's reason for reporting is the justice engine's weighing (duty, traits, tie); the lines say only what the records show: who saw it or was told, whether the money was taken, and how close the two are.
why: The investigation weighs the crime and the complaint, not a conversation between the accuser and the accused. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A justice-engine reading of what the accused told the accuser (a disclosure or a confession to a witness) as evidence or mitigation.

whatItFakes: What the relative who comes to see a new baby offers or asks (dinner, the dishes, an hour of sleep, to hold the baby) is worded for every birth; nothing on a record says this relative will bring dinner. The child's name, the other parent, and the visitor's town (when it is not the parent's) are from the birth record and the people records.
why: No engine keeps what a visitor brings to a new parent; the visit is the purpose itself, and its lines name only things any relative might offer. Resolved Nov 10, 2026 (stand-in triage): dropped as too in depth (owner); the estimate stays as the game's answer.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A wants record per person and the household's chores and sleep from the people engine, so the visit offers what the home needs.

whatItFakes: A job found, lost or left is told as a small story from the past-work records. An official's referral is on record and employers read it, but the hire keeps no referral, so the entry never says who helped, and the feeling in it is only what the pay comparison supports.
why: The past-work spells keep no referral, no search and no mood; naming a helper or a feeling the records do not hold would be invented.
replacement: A referral and a search on the jobs engine's seeker and hire records, read when a past or played job starts, so the entry can say who made the difference.

whatItFakes: The outline rows for a victory, a concession and a swearing-in exist, but those speeches are still worded by their own paths and do not go through planSpeech. A council or board member's floor speech and a local campaign speech now go through it (local-speeches.ts); the player's own built speech (speech-builder.ts) does not yet.
why: Unit 3's time box (Nov 12) covered the planner and the addresses of the President, governors and mayors; the other kinds need their banks typed by section first.
replacement: Each of those speeches calls planSpeech with its row, and its own planner or joiner is deleted.

whatItFakes: The theme weights (speech-outlines.json theme) are first guesses: in ten drawn worlds on Nov 12 the President's address led with paying for a higher debt limit in six, because the macro year is nearly the same in every world and the taxes-finance subject holds the one open federal question most Presidents stand far from the center on.
why: Unit 3's time box ran out before the weights were tuned against draws.
replacement: Weights tuned so no question leads more than half of ten drawn addresses; the half-draws assertion in speech-outline.test.ts turned on.

whatItFakes: A policy question the laws engine holds no row for in a jurisdiction is read as open (no law answers it yes), cited by the powers record, so a speaker can ask for it. On Nov 12, 11 of the 23 federal questions (a higher top income tax rate, defense spending, foreign aid, a national loan-interest cap, passenger rail and others) had no starting row.
why: Every President spoke to the same twelve federal questions, so the same three asks led every address (owner: "why is it always stock trading?").
replacement: The laws engine seeds a starting row for every federal question (in force or not, from the record), and this default is deleted.

whatItFakes: A speaker's earlier addresses are found by reading the durable log for address records that name them as speaker, once each time an address is composed (a few times a year), instead of through an index by speaker.
why: The one writer of every address prefers the wordings a voice has not used in its earlier addresses, and no record lists a speaker's addresses with the pieces they were said with.
replacement: The speech module's addresses table (bySpeaker) keeps each address with its pieces, and this read uses its index.

whatItFakes: A governor's or local head's opening tells the budget's balance (budgets.ts), a law of the jurisdiction that took effect in the past year (the laws engine) or a disaster declared for the place (disasters.ts), but no change in jobs or in a big employer: no engine keeps a town's or a state's own year-over-year jobs record the speech could cite, and the outcome web's term read holds no months in a world's first year.
why: The words lead, Nov 12: no speech named anything that happened in its place. The budget, the laws and the disasters are read now (words builder, Nov 12); the jobs reader waits on its engine.
replacement: The planner reads the jobs record of the speaker's realm (a town's employers, a state's jobs) once an engine keeps it by year, and the term read once it holds months.

whatItFakes: A town's, township's or county's officeholder or candidate has no signature issues: the officials engine draws a few causes of their own only for the officials it keeps a row for (state and federal), so a local speaker's theme is picked from how strongly they hold each view and what their traits pull toward, never from causes of their own.
why: Local officeholders are full people read through the one stance engine (campaign-stances.ts stanceReader); giving them causes needs the officials engine's drawn signature for local seats.
replacement: The officials engine draws a local officeholder's signature issues when they take a local seat (pool item core-local-official-signature), and standsOfPerson reads them.

whatItFakes: Where a local government seats no mayor or county executive and its body has not yet chosen whoever presides (no leadership post held), the member who has served longest gives the local address.
why: The leadership engine organizes a body the first time a post is read; a board it has not organized has no chair on record.
replacement: The leadership engine organizes every local body at the opening, and the address reads its presiding officer only.

whatItFakes: The floor-debate scene and the scene after a candidate's stump speech play the speech composed by the one planner (speechOfRecord) only for a town's, township's or county's body and race; a state or federal chamber's floor debate still opens on its talk line, and a state or federal candidate's speech is not played.
why: composeFloorSpeech and composeCampaignSpeech read the town's seats (townSeats); a state legislator's or a congressional candidate's speech needs the officials engine's row as the governor's address reads it (words builder, Nov 12).
replacement: composeFloorSpeech and composeCampaignSpeech read any chamber's members and any race's office through the officials engine, and the floor-debate talk lines that open the scene are deleted.

whatItFakes: The player's own campaign speech is the stage builder's four picked parts, each said on its own, not planned by the one outline planner, and a player seated on a town body has no floor speech of their own.
why: Wiring the stage choices into planSpeech is more than this pull request's hour (words builder, Nov 12); pool item words-player-speech-through-planner.
replacement: Each stage offers the planner's points for the player's stands and /give composes the speech from the plan; the floor day offers the player composeFloorSpeech.

whatItFakes: The State of the Union, the State of the State, a mayor's address and a candidate's campaign speech route through the one outline planner (src/english/outline-planner.ts, src/director/address-telling.ts) where their outline banks can say a required section; the old composer (the old point shapes and composeBlocks) stands in until the national and local speeches writers fill them.
why: The owner's plan of Nov 24 (via the CTO): one stretch, the first evening, until he says it is right in the installed game; nothing else is rewritten before then.
replacement: Each address kind gets its outline row and pieces in the planner's bank, and composeBlocks, pointShapes and the old opening-speech pieces are deleted.

whatItFakes: The sentence that opens a Journal chapter (a birth or the player's own move) is told by the one outline planner's journal-chapter-open row (src/director/journal-chapter-open.ts) where its bank, data/english/parts/outline-journal.json, can say it; where it cannot, the Journal's row composer and its mined journal.json lines stand in.
why: The owner's plan of Nov 24 (via the CTO): one stretch, the first evening, until he says it is right in the installed game; the outline-journal bank is seeded with the row composer's own opener lines until the Journal writer fills it (#9750, 7135335379).
addedBy: Story helper, for the Story lead, Nov 24
replacement: The Journal writer fills outline-journal for every chapter-opening move, every chapter-opening moment goes through the planner, and the row composer's opener lines and this fallback are deleted.
